8 questions. Click an answer to check it: you will see right away whether it is correct, with a short explanation. Nothing is saved.

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**1.** What is the first principal component?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- The original variable with the largest variance
- The direction along which the projected data has the largest variance
- The direction that best separates the classes
- The average of all the variables
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
PCA turns an axis through the centre of the cloud and keeps the direction where the projections are the most spread out. It is a combination of all the variables, and PCA never uses the labels.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**2.** What is on the diagonal of a covariance matrix?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- The correlations between pairs of variables
- The variance of each variable
- Only zeros
- The means of the variables
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
The diagonal holds the variances; the other cells hold the covariances between pairs of variables. The matrix is symmetric because Cov(x, y) = Cov(y, x).
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="2"}
**3.** In PCA, what does the eigenvalue of a component tell you?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- The angle of the component
- The number of variables that drive the component
- The variance of the data along this component
- The accuracy of a model trained on this component
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
If C u = λ u with u of length 1, then the variance of the projections, uᵀ C u, is equal to λ. scikit-learn stores the eigenvalues in `explained_variance_`, and their shares in `explained_variance_ratio_`.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="2"}
**4.** What does the covariance matrix of the principal components look like?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- The same as the covariance matrix of the original variables
- All its values are equal to 1
- It is diagonal: the components are uncorrelated, and the diagonal holds the eigenvalues
- It is full of large negative values
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
PCA rotates the cloud so that its axes become the new variables. They are uncorrelated, sorted by decreasing variance, and the total variance is unchanged.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**5.** A dataset has a `price` column in euros (values in the thousands) and a `rating` from 1 to 5. What happens if you run a PCA without standardising?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- Nothing, PCA is not sensitive to the units
- The first component will be almost only `price`, because its variance is much larger
- PCA will fail with an error
- The first component will be almost only `rating`
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
PCA looks for variance, and a variable in large units has a large variance just because of its unit. Standardise first, unless all the variables share the same unit and their spread is meaningful (like the pixels of an image).
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="2"}
**6.** `PCA(n_components=0.9)` means...

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- Keep 90% of the variables
- Keep 9 components
- Keep the smallest number of components that explains at least 90% of the variance
- Drop the components that explain less than 0.9% of the variance
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
An integer gives the number of components; a float between 0 and 1 gives the share of variance to keep. After fitting, `n_components_` tells how many components were kept.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**7.** You keep 5 components out of 20 and call `inverse_transform`. What do you get?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- The original data, exactly
- An approximation of the original data, rebuilt from the 5 components only
- The 5 components
- The covariance matrix
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
`inverse_transform` goes back to the original variables: x̂ = mean + z₁u₁ + … + z₅u₅. The error comes from the 15 dropped components: its size is the variance they carried.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="2"}
**8.** Why can PCA remove noise from images?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- Because it deletes the pixels with the most noise
- Because it standardises the pixels
- Because the noise spreads evenly over all the components, while the shapes of the images are concentrated in the first ones
- Because the labels tell PCA which pixels are noise
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
Random noise has no favourite direction. The signal (the strokes of the digits) is strongly correlated between pixels, so a few components hold most of it. Keeping these components and rebuilding the images with `inverse_transform` removes most of the noise.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-score}
